general.temas: Recurring topics include the debate over pensions in Germany, politics in Saxony-Anhalt, the formation of a government in Israel and the disturbances at the Beşiktaş-Hapoel match. Also featured are the winter storm, the succession at the ECB and the controversy over Jamal Musiala at Bayern. Only taz highlights the call for a study of sexism in the police.
general.motivo_crispacion: Tensions are high because of the clash between the Union and the SPD over pensions, as well as disputes in Saxony-Anhalt over the AfD. The disturbances at the Beşiktaş-Hapoel match, linked to the Gaza war, and internal criticism within the CDU also feature prominently. Some front pages use harsh language and speak of scandals. Partly offsetting this atmosphere are the pay agreement between IG Metall and employers and sports or weather stories without political conflict.

Süddeutsche Zeitung.resumen:
- The US delays a decision on its troops in Europe.
- An IG Metall agreement provides for pay rises of 4.3% and flexibility measures conditional on investment and jobs.
- Eisenkot reaches a coalition agreement in Israel; Hernández de Cos will succeed Lagarde as head of the ECB.
- The Archdiocese of Cologne must pay 550,000 euros over sexual abuse; Depardieu will stand trial for an alleged rape.
- The front page also covers political debate, Bayern and Musiala, renewable energy, snow and birds.
Süddeutsche Zeitung.motivo_populismo: An informative tone predominates, although expressions such as “Shitbürgertums” and “the joke of the year” introduce disparagement and sensationalist emphasis.
Süddeutsche Zeitung.sesgo: The coverage takes a favourable view of dialogue in the labour agreement and is critical of Poschardt, Kurz and Bayern's handling of Musiala. The selection combines politics, economics and the courts with sports, the environment and everyday life.

Die Welt.resumen:
- The left calls for new elections in Saxony-Anhalt; the AfD pushes for a vote to elect the regional head of government.
- The AfD gains an additional seat in the Federal Convention after a secret ballot in Berlin; a change to the broadcasting committee's rules also draws criticism.
- Early retirement divides the governing parties and draws criticism from experts.
- The coverage addresses extremism among young Muslims and the investigation of an alleged sexual assault attributed to four young Syrians.
- Rounding out the front page are disturbances at a match, the winter storm, Heckler & Koch's results and a Musk satellite project.
Die Welt.motivo_populismo: Alarmist or sensationalist expressions abound, such as “scandal”, “the great pension drama” and “the gradual abolition of democracy”, as well as disparaging phrases such as “exceptionally stupid proposals”.
Die Welt.sesgo: The front page prioritises political conflict and presents the dispute over pensions and the change to broadcasting rules in particularly dramatic terms. It also highlights religion or nationality in stories about extremism and an alleged sexual assault.

Der Spiegel.resumen:
- The Union proposes a compromise on pensions, prompting an irritated reaction from the SPD.
- SAP suffers a cyberattack; major companies call for reforms as rail transport costs rise.
- Coalition talks in Israel and the European dispute over agricultural subsidies draw international attention.
- A study raises the possibility of cooperation between Russia and Iran against Europe; a trial over alleged spying for Russia begins in Berlin.
- The front page also covers prostitution, mental health, a storm in the US and two football stories.
Der Spiegel.motivo_populismo: Expressions such as “the Union catches the SPD off guard”, “major companies lash out” and “suffers conspicuously” dramatise some events, but there is no systematic appeal to the people against the elites.
Der Spiegel.sesgo: The selection highlights political, economic and security conflicts and presents the corporate perspective on rail costs. On prostitution, it takes an explicit stance against banning the purchase of sex; no clear overall political orientation emerges.

Bild.resumen:
- Bayern will build a new stadium for its women's team at a cost of 80 million euros.
- The front page brings together sports stories about the Bears, Leverkusen, Dortmund, Germany's under-21 team and Simon Wulff's return to bobsleigh.
- The arrival of winter in the south causes traffic problems and the closure of the motorway towards the Brenner Pass.
- A Bavarian brewer recalls beer over incorrect labelling: it contains alcohol despite being presented as alcohol-free.
- Andreas Dahlmeier speaks about the death of his daughter Laura, and chef Gordon Ramsay becomes a grandfather.
Bild.motivo_populismo: Alarmist and sensationalist expressions such as “Schock”, “Horror-Gruppe” and “Chaos” abound, although there is no evident opposition between the people and the elites.
Bild.sesgo: The selection prioritises sport, especially football, and combines incidents, celebrities and consumer news. The writing favours emotional impact and curiosity over a strictly informative tone.

taz.resumen:
- Possible cooperation between the BSW and the AfD generates internal tensions.
- The Greens call for a study of sexism in the police.
- Rebels advance in an Ebola-affected area of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
- The front page criticises tax advantages for the wealthy and companies and the invitation extended to a former Mossad chief to visit the Bundestag.
- It also covers pesticides, the arms industry, a labour dispute and the succession at the ECB.
taz.motivo_populismo: Expressions such as “scandal”, “martial spectacle” and “loopholes for the ultra-rich”, together with the call “let's get to work!”, add judgment and drama, although an explicit appeal to the people against the elites does not predominate.
taz.sesgo: The selection and wording show a critical approach to the far right, the arms industry and tax privileges for the wealthy and companies. They also give prominence to issues of sexism, public health and workers' rights.

opiniones.comunista:
I welcome the fact that IG Metall has secured a 4.3% pay rise for millions of industrial workers. But the agreement also allows temporary pay cuts or longer working hours without compensation, in exchange for investment and job guarantees. We should not accept as natural that those who live by their labour should bear the risk of business decisions.

The discussion about pensions raises the same question: who pays? I reject resolving it by cutting rights while, according to the revelations about Deutsche Bank, tax loopholes remain for the wealthy and companies. I support closing those loopholes and strengthening pensions and public services. And in the face of the industrial crisis, I want investment under democratic control and collective ownership: it is not enough to ask big capital to invest; the working class must be able to decide what is produced and for whom.
opiniones.anarquista:
The IG Metall agreement brings a 4.3% pay rise, but it also accepts temporary pay cuts or longer working hours without compensation in exchange for investment and jobs. I do not disparage negotiation: I know that organised solidarity wins improvements. I wonder, however, why workers must give up time and pay so that others can decide how investment is made. I want unions controlled from below and companies run by their workers, not a democracy that stops at the factory gate.

In Fuchstal, a network has managed to restart using wind and solar power and batteries. I see a possibility there, not an accomplished revolution: communities governing their energy and sharing resources through mutual aid. Collective freedom begins when we stop depending on distant hierarchies to make decisions about our lives.
opiniones.liberal:
The agreement between IG Metall and employers strikes me as good news: it shows that workers and companies can negotiate pay and flexibility without waiting for the state to dictate every solution. The 4.3% increase comes alongside temporary adjustments subject to investment and employment commitments. That autonomy does not eliminate conflicts, but it makes it possible to address them responsibly.

I also see a missed opportunity in the European dispute over agricultural subsidies: instead of fighting over how to distribute more public money, governments should reduce subsidies, cut spending and lower taxes. A freer market rewards innovation better than budgetary privileges do.

And the debate about retirement demands honesty: promises must be sustainable, without shifting rising costs onto workers. I prefer clear rules, personal responsibility and a limited state that protects rights, rather than deciding for us.
opiniones.extrema_derecha:
The US delay in deciding what to do about its troops in Europe reminds me of an uncomfortable truth: Germany cannot entrust its security indefinitely to decisions made in Washington. I want strong national defence and a foreign policy based on our interests, not the convenience of allies or bureaucrats.

I am also concerned about the dispute over European agricultural subsidies. The countryside is not just another budget item: it sustains communities, traditions and an essential part of our autonomy. And I welcome the fact that unions and employers have reached an agreement in industry, although the sacrifices it entails warrant scrutiny: protecting productive employment must be a national priority. On migration, I support strict controls and demanding integration requirements, compatible with the rule of law. Security and sovereignty are not extremist slogans: they are basic obligations of any responsible government.
opiniones.centro:
I see a lesson in democratic politics in the agreement between IG Metall and employers: negotiating does not mean abandoning principles, but recognising that an industry in crisis needs decent wages as well as investment and jobs. The 4.3% rise comes with difficult concessions, conditional on commitments from companies. That balance warrants scrutiny, but it is preferable to turning every conflict into a deadlocked test of strength.

I would like to see the same willingness in the debate over pensions. The new attempt at a compromise should be judged on its ability to protect those who have worked for decades while sustaining the system for future generations. Neither unfunded promises nor indiscriminate cuts constitute responsible reform. Governing requires explaining the costs, listening and gradually correcting what does not work.
